title: At the Limits of Computability: Steps Towards Autonomous AI Discovery on the Busy Beaver Frontier
authors: Marco Dos Santos, Vivek Veeriah, Alex Havrilla, Andrew Bolt, Goran Zuzic, Satinder Singh
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in AI for mathematics---ranging from Olympiad medal performances to resolving long-standing open conjectures---have rapidly expanded what automated systems can achieve. Yet these successes primarily concern predefined, human-formulated problems, leaving open how AI systems can autonomously uncover mathematical structure and formulate new questions. To push beyond static challenges, we explore the Busy Beaver (BB) domain, an uncomputable frontier that is fundamentally open-ended. Because no algorithm can compute the Busy Beaver number $\mathrm{BB}(n)$ for every $n$, this domain provides a natural setting for sustained exploration through mathematical conjecture and proof. In this paper, we introduce a Gemini-based agentic pipeline that automatically discovers accelerations of Turing machines, expressed as compact mathematical rules summarizing many execution steps. Our system integrates pattern recognition, automated conjecturing, informal mathematical reasoning, and formal theorem proving in Lean. With this framework, our system autonomously discovered and formally verified novel Collatz-like accelerations for eleven machines in $\mathrm{BB}(6)$. Subject to community acceptance, we provisionally classify these machines as Cryptids, namely machines whose blank-tape executions admit exact, compact mathematical descriptions but whose halting behavior remains unresolved. These results advance the analysis of $\mathrm{BB}(6)$ holdouts on the Busy Beaver frontier and demonstrate the potential of autonomous AI systems for open-ended mathematical discovery in fundamental computer science.

infographic.key_insight: A Gemini-based agent autonomously discovered and formally verified compact, Collatz-like execution rules for eleven BB(6) Turing machines without resolving their halting behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work demonstrates a workflow for turning AI-generated patterns into machine-checked mathematical results in an open-ended computational domain.
method: Recognize patterns in Turing-machine execution and conjecture compact acceleration rules.
Use informal mathematical reasoning to develop candidate proofs.

infographic.watch_item: Verified acceleration rules do not establish whether these machines halt, and the abstract provides no aggregate success rate or computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: At the Limits of Computability: Steps Towards Autonomous AI Discovery on the Busy Beaver Frontier

title: Corrected Block Sparse Spectral Optimization: Exact Models, Finite Identification, and Local Dynamics
authors: Omid Shams Solari
abstract: The block generalized-power method pairs threshold-based support selection with inexpensive Stiefel updates, but the standard block formulation conflates two nonequivalent objectives and leaves inactive components, threshold ties, and post-selection refitting ill-specified. We rebuild the model from the primal. Eliminating each loading column from the normalized loading-ball problem gives a sum of soft-thresholded Euclidean norms (A-SUM); the squared-threshold objective in common use arises from a quadratic lift (A-SQ). We prove both identities, exhibit a two-component instance whose maximizers disagree, and specify explicit conventions for zero-response columns, ties, rank deficiency, and mask-before-refit. For A-SQ we separate the historical full-polar iteration from a safeguarded Riemannian ascent and prove, for the latter, whole-sequence convergence via a sufficient-ascent lemma, a relative-error lemma, and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, which applies because the soft-threshold objective and the Stiefel constraint are semi-algebraic. A strict threshold margin then forces finite identification of the support and sign pattern. The post-identification map is ordinary power iteration on the active covariance for a rank-one hard threshold, and the Frechet derivative of a coupled polar map for component-specific supports; a radius-based safe-screening rule follows from the same local analysis. Planted-spike experiments match the predicted identification time and local rates. On modern-AI panels (GPT-2 residual stream, ViT CLS stream, Pitprops) the thresholded block-sparse components match dense PCA on reconstruction and improve on it in monosemanticity and class specialisation. On three native-label scRNA datasets (Zheng17 FACS-sorted PBMCs, 68k donor-A with FACS-correlated labels, Tabula Muris) A-SQ beats dense PCA on cluster-recovery AMI by +0.023 to +0.044 at matched sparsity.

infographic.key_insight: Two commonly conflated block-sparse objectives have different exact models and can yield different maximizers; safeguarded A-SQ ascent supports convergence and finite support identification under a strict threshold margin.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The corrected formulation provides a principled basis for sparse feature extraction, with explicit edge-case handling and locally justified safe screening.
method: Derive A-SUM from normalized loading balls and A-SQ from a quadratic lift.
Use safeguarded Riemannian ascent on the Stiefel manifold, with explicit tie, zero-response, rank-deficiency, and refitting conventions.
Analyze post-identification dynamics using active-covariance power iteration or a coupled polar-map derivative.
infographic.evidence_signal: Planted-spike tests match predicted identification times and local rates; AI-panel tests report PCA-level reconstruction with improved interpretability, while three scRNA datasets show AMI gains of 0.023–0.044 over dense PCA at matched sparsity.
infographic.watch_item: The convergence guarantee applies to safeguarded ascent, not the historical full-polar iteration, and finite support identification requires a strict threshold margin.
infographic.paper_title: Corrected Block Sparse Spectral Optimization: Exact Models, Finite Identification, and Local Dynamics

title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
authors: Maria-Eleni Sfyraki, Jun-Kun Wang
abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes stochastic first- and zeroth-order optimization methods for training on a mix of ground-truth and potentially incorrect ML-generated labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could reduce dependence on costly human labeling when scaling model training.
method: Combine samples with ground-truth labels and samples labeled by an ML predictor.
Develop stochastic first-order optimization methods for mixed-label training.
Develop stochastic zeroth-order optimization methods for the same setting.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports empirical studies ranging from linear regression training to LLM fine-tuning, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness to different rates and patterns of ML-label errors is not specified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization

title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
authors: Ruotian Peng, Yuanyi Ren, Shuaiqi Liu, Xin Guo, Fang Zhu, Yangyi Huang
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTrainingBench.

infographic.key_insight: VibeTraining-Bench evaluates whether research agents can improve target agent systems by jointly refining training data, trainers, and inference harnesses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark tests coordinated training-and-inference optimization under fixed resource budgets rather than isolated component tuning.
method: Start from identical initial systems within each task and use validation feedback to guide iterative improvements.

infographic.paper_title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement

title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
authors: Haoyu Li, Zeren Shui, Yuhao Zhang, Ferhat Erata, Benjamin Mikek, Murali Krishna Ramanathan
abstract: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof obligations into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.

infographic.key_insight: Maestro improves Lean proof development by diagnosing failures and revising the global proof plan instead of repeatedly decomposing stuck lemmas.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its coordination approach extends to verified code synthesis, where checked counterexamples trigger code repair.
method: Provers report why attempts failed, not just that they failed.

infographic.paper_title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination

title: Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization for Reasoning Language Models
authors: Hui Yang, Wan Tian, Tao Ren, Zhongyi Li, Yijie Peng
abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.

infographic.key_insight: CSPO adaptively calibrates sequence-level policy clipping to target a marginal tail budget as reasoning-model training evolves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive clipping offers a way to align policy-update constraints with whole-response rewards while accounting for changing score distributions.
method: Calibrate sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics.
Target a specified marginal miscoverage level, with explicit corrections for CDF discrepancy and policy drift.
Under additional moment conditions, bound objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series report improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints adapting during training.
infographic.watch_item: Marginal calibration does not guarantee calibration conditional on response length; that requires additional assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization for Reasoning Language Models

title: Distributional Lifting for Discrete Optimization
authors: Ningji Wei, Jiaming Liang
abstract: We introduce a framework that transforms discrete optimization into continuous optimization over parameterized probability distributions. The framework reveals a common distributional structure behind several methods that have largely developed independently, including continuous reformulations for multilinear binary optimization, Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning, the cross-entropy method, mean-field variational optimization, and the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. It enables flexible and modular algorithm design, for example, by using neural networks to incorporate contextual information or by enforcing convexity of the lifted problem. We establish two theoretical results: a link between the lifted optimality gap and sampling quality in the original discrete problem, and a convergence guarantee for the lifted optimization problem under suitable conditions. These results lead to a unified algorithmic template based on batched sampling and stochastic gradient updates that is naturally compatible with GPU computation. We demonstrate the framework through three case studies spanning multidimensional knapsack, covering-constrained three-dimensional assignment, and a stochastic mixed-integer location-allocation problem, showing that it can accommodate distinct combinatorial structures and scale to large discrete and mixed-integer settings.

infographic.key_insight: Distributional lifting transforms discrete optimization into continuous optimization over parameterized probability distributions, unifying several established approaches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports modular, GPU-compatible solvers for combinatorial and mixed-integer problems, with options to incorporate context through neural networks.
method: Optimize parameterized distributions over discrete solutions.
Use batched sampling and stochastic gradient updates.

infographic.watch_item: Convergence guarantees require suitable conditions, so their applicability must be checked for each distribution parameterization and problem.
infographic.paper_title: Distributional Lifting for Discrete Optimization

title: Newton-Based Methods for Bilevel Optimization Beyond Lower-Level Strong Convexity
authors: Youran Dong, Junfeng Yang, Wei Yao, Jin Zhang
abstract: Bilevel optimization provides a framework for machine learning tasks such as hyperparameter optimization, data reweighting, and meta-learning. Existing Newton-based bilevel methods typically rely on the classical hypergradient formula, which is generally unavailable when lower-level solutions are nonunique and the lower-level Hessian is singular. We develop two Newton-based methods beyond lower-level strong convexity by exploiting curvature shared by the lower-level and multiplier updates. Newton-based GALET handles potentially singular lower-level curvature under a positive spectral-gap condition, exploiting its range structure to avoid the squared-Hessian multiplier system used in GALET. Newton-based BAMM uses a strongly convex aggregation model when the lower-level objective is convex and the upper-level objective is strongly convex in the lower-level variable. We establish convergence guarantees and improved complexity bounds relative to GALET and sl-BAMM under the corresponding assumptions. We further introduce GNBO, a generalized Newton-based framework that captures the shared-curvature structure of the proposed methods and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods. Experiments on synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and GPT-2 data reweighting evaluate the proposed methods across different bilevel learning tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Shared curvature enables Newton-based bilevel optimization beyond lower-level strong convexity, including settings with nonunique solutions and singular Hessians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The methods target hyperparameter optimization, data reweighting, and meta-learning when classical hypergradient formulas may be unavailable.
method: Newton-based GALET exploits Hessian range structure under a positive spectral gap, avoiding GALET’s squared-Hessian multiplier system.
Newton-based BAMM uses a strongly convex aggregation model when the lower objective is convex and the upper objective is strongly convex in the lower variable.
GNBO unifies the shared-curvature structure of these methods and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports convergence guarantees and improved complexity bounds over GALET and sl-BAMM under corresponding assumptions, plus evaluations on synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and GPT-2 data reweighting.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees remain assumption-dependent: removing lower-level strong convexity does not remove spectral-gap or other convexity requirements.
infographic.paper_title: Newton-Based Methods for Bilevel Optimization Beyond Lower-Level Strong Convexity

title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Zikun Qu, Jiahang Sun, Xiangyi Wang, Zhiwei Shang
abstract: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.

infographic.key_insight: IF-MAP prioritizes agents by their estimated potential to improve end-to-end performance, rather than by responsibility for failures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Teams can focus prompt optimization or model upgrades on promising agents instead of spending resources improving every agent.
method: Probe each agent with controlled semantic prompt perturbations and measure end-to-end loss changes.
Fit a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace.
Rank agents by estimated response norm without accessing model parameters or gradients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six workflows spanning coding, question answering, and math, prioritized prompt optimization gained 3.81 percentage points versus 1.85 for uniform selection; upgrades across five target models gained 7.62–16.42 points versus 3.81–8.62.
infographic.watch_item: Probing adds overhead, and local sensitivity to prompt perturbations may not reliably predict gains from every subsequent intervention.
infographic.paper_title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems

title: A Deep Backward Scheme for Reflected BSDEs via Penalization : Approximation and Convergence Analysis
authors: E. H. Essaky, M. A. Jalal, Y. Ouknine
abstract: We propose and analyze a deep backward numerical scheme for Markovian reflected backward stochastic differential equations with a generator independent of the control variable, based on the penalization method. The reflection constraint is replaced by penalized BSDEs, which are approximated backward in time by neural networks, with particular attention to the dependence of the errors on the penalization parameter \(λ\). We derive quantitative error estimates for both the value process \(Y\) and the control process \(Z\). A key ingredient is an \(L^2\)-regularity estimate for the control component with explicit dependence on \(λ\). Exploiting the monotonicity of the penalization term, we obtain stability estimates uniform in \(λ\) and prove uniform spatial Lipschitz bounds for both the penalized value functions and the discrete backward targets. Consequently, the GroupSort Lipschitz constraints and the associated neural-network approximation error can be controlled uniformly in \(λ\). The global analysis separates penalization, time-discretization, forward, and neural-network approximation errors. Balancing the dominant terms yields a mean-square error of order \(O(|π|^{1/3})\) for the value component, together with a corresponding estimate for a post-training reconstruction of \(Z\). Numerical experiments with an explicit reflected BSDE and American option problems illustrate the scheme on one-dimensional and structured high-dimensional benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: A penalization-based deep backward scheme approximates reflected BSDEs with a proven value-process mean-square error of O(|π|^{1/3}) after balancing dominant errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The scheme offers a theoretically controlled neural approach to constrained stochastic models, including American option valuation.
method: Replace reflection with penalized BSDEs and approximate backward in time using neural networks.
Use monotonicity to establish stability and spatial Lipschitz bounds uniform in the penalty parameter.
Separate penalization, time-discretization, forward, and neural approximation errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative error estimates for Y and Z, plus numerical experiments on an explicit reflected BSDE and American options in one-dimensional and structured high-dimensional settings.
infographic.watch_item: The analysis assumes a generator independent of the control variable Z, limiting direct applicability to more general reflected BSDEs.
infographic.paper_title: A Deep Backward Scheme for Reflected BSDEs via Penalization : Approximation and Convergence Analysis

title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
authors: Jean-Loup Dupret, Patrick Cheridito
abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

infographic.key_insight: Deep Pontryagin learning separates adjoint estimation from policy improvement to solve high-dimensional stochastic control problems with jump-diffusions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets continuous-time decision systems with random fluctuations and abrupt jumps without repeatedly differentiating the objective through the full dynamics during policy updates.
method: Simulate trajectories under a fixed Markov control and backpropagate rewards to generate pathwise adjoint labels.
Regress adjoint labels onto the Markov state using supervised learning.
Update the control via pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors prove a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and continuous-time adjoint convergence, while numerical experiments illustrate accuracy, stability, and scalability without quantitative details in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance may depend on trajectory coverage and adjoint regression quality, especially when important jumps are rare.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps

title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories
authors: Xinyue Peng, Zhenlin Liang, Meng Cai, Hua Wang
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.

infographic.key_insight: GLOBE uses the geometry of reasoning trajectories to stop chain-of-thought generation early, reducing computation while maintaining performance comparable to full reasoning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This online, training-free approach could lower inference costs and latency in mathematical reasoning, tool-calling, and agent-memory workloads.
method: Embed each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere.

infographic.watch_item: Confidence thresholds and trajectory stopping criteria may need validation on new models and tasks to avoid premature exits.
infographic.paper_title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories

title: Beyond Leaderboards: A Method for Application-Specific Capability Profiling of Large Language Models
authors: Oleg Grynets, Vasyl Lyashkevych, Andrii Salyk, Dmytro Koziuberda, Dmytro Kostetskyi, Oleh Kaskun
abstract: Public leaderboards rank large language models (LLMs) in general, but an engineer has to choose a model for a specific application, architecture and cost. This paper presents a method for application-specific capability profiling of LLMs and its realization as a containerized testbed. The method treats each application as a unit of extension: an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration agent, a documentation-grounded chatbot or an enterprise-support automation agent runs in its own container behind a small contract, brings its own dataset, evaluator and owned attributes, and is onboarded together with its dashboards. Measurements accumulate in a versioned, sparse metamodel of every model. The method separates the model under test from judges and agents, freezes and hashes plans, refuses to compare values from different contexts, diagnoses the instrument before the system, and applies a null-agent check and a noise rule whose operating characteristics are quantified by simulation. In the evaluated automation conditions, model choices produced larger differences on selected observable outcomes than framework choices, although the experimental design does not establish a general causal ranking of these factors. The experiments also show that instruction tuning is deployment-specific and that system-reported success can exceed independently observed success: of 216 migration units checked against a real Oracle database, 108 were demonstrably correct. These measurements establish application-specific observations, not a universal model ranking.

infographic.key_insight: Choose LLMs using application-specific capability profiles rather than universal leaderboard rankings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A containerized testbed helps engineers evaluate models within their intended application, architecture, and cost context.
method: Package each application with its own dataset, evaluator, attributes, and dashboards behind a shared contract.
Accumulate measurements in versioned, sparse model profiles using frozen, hashed plans and context-matched comparisons.
Separate tested models from judges and agents; validate the test instrument with null-agent checks and a simulation-characterized noise rule.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 216 migration units checked against a real Oracle database, 108 were demonstrably correct, showing why reported success requires independent verification.
infographic.watch_item: Results are application-specific, and the experimental design does not establish a general causal ranking of model versus framework effects.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Leaderboards: A Method for Application-Specific Capability Profiling of Large Language Models

title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management
authors: Marco Boresta, Tommaso Giovannelli, Sepehr Namirad, Giulia Riccardi
abstract: Multi-criteria models for healthcare operations need weights that express how stakeholders trade off patient waiting time, provider workload, and operating cost, but these weights are difficult to quantify. Teams of large language model (LLM) agents, each prompted to represent a stakeholder, have been used to supply them. We propose a framework for assessing the reliability of LLM-generated preferences as inputs to multi-objective optimization and quantifying how their uncertainty affects decisions. We study explicit preferences by asking agents to rate the importance of the criteria in an outpatient appointment scheduling problem, and implicit preferences by inferring trade-offs from the agents' pairwise choices between emergency department configurations. The computational experiments show that the explicit preferences respond to the clinic's operating conditions and differ across roles, but deliberation among the agents can erase these differences, whereas simple averaging preserves them. The pairwise choices used to reveal the agents' implicit preferences depend largely on which option is presented first, and we find limited evidence that a statistical model using contextual information alongside presentation order predicts the agents' choices on new comparison pairs better than a model using presentation order alone. We then formulate robust weighted-sum optimization models to account for preference uncertainty. In most cases, these models select different schedules or configurations from those obtained using average preference weights. These results indicate that LLM-generated preferences need an audit of this kind before they are used as optimization weights in healthcare decision support.

infographic.key_insight: LLM stakeholder preferences can reflect healthcare operating conditions, but deliberation and option order can distort them and change optimization decisions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Healthcare decision-support systems should audit LLM-generated weights and account for preference uncertainty before optimizing schedules or service configurations.
method: Elicit explicit criterion ratings from stakeholder agents for outpatient appointment scheduling.
Infer implicit trade-offs from pairwise choices between emergency department configurations.
Evaluate preference reliability and use robust weighted-sum optimization to handle uncertainty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Computational experiments found that deliberation could erase role differences, pairwise choices depended largely on presentation order, and robust models usually selected different solutions than average-weight models.
infographic.watch_item: Context-aware choice models showed limited evidence of better prediction on new comparison pairs than presentation-order-only models.
infographic.paper_title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management

title: VoxLogicA2: A Spatial Model Checker for Neuro-symbolic Medical Imaging (extended version)
authors: Gina Belmonte, Laura Bussi, Vincenzo Ciancia, Mieke Massink
abstract: We present the tool VoxLogicA2, a spatial model checker aimed at Computer Vision, with applications in high-resolution 2D and 3D medical imaging. The new version of the tool combines logical primitives, non-logical primitives, and training and prediction primitives of state-of-the-art neural networks, freely interleaved with the symbolic tool functionality. The primary application field is neuro-symbolic medical image analysis. VoxLogicA2 is a fast, parallelising spatial model checker with a declarative domain-specific language, capable of describing both the learning procedures and the spatial logic procedures of an analysis in one program. We validate our approach by verifying its improved efficiency, and by using the new constructs of the language to describe case studies of previous work, which were based on Python, with a specification that uses VoxLogicA2 only

infographic.key_insight: VoxLogicA2 unifies spatial logic and neural-network training and prediction in one declarative language for neuro-symbolic medical image analysis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can express learning workflows and symbolic spatial analysis together for high-resolution 2D and 3D images using a parallelising model checker.
method: Interleave logical, non-logical, and neural-network primitives.
Specify learning and spatial analysis in one declarative program.
Execute image-analysis workflows with parallel spatial model checking.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved efficiency and reimplementation of previously Python-based case studies entirely in VoxLogicA2, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and integration costs need assessment on target imaging workloads; the abstract does not specify hardware requirements or benchmark details.
infographic.paper_title: VoxLogicA2: A Spatial Model Checker for Neuro-symbolic Medical Imaging (extended version)

title: Exploring Visual Access and Proactive AI Tutoring for Handwritten Mathematics
authors: Nachiket Kotalwar, Conrad Borchers, Shubham Gandhi, Partha Sarathi Purkayastha, David Yaron, Carolyn P. Rosé
abstract: Handwritten work captures mathematical reasoning that learners may not express in typed or voice-dictated messages. We built a multimodal AI tutoring platform in which a phone camera gives the tutor a live view of learners' work on paper. In a randomized online study, 117 adults solved calculus problems with Text-Reactive, Visual-Reactive, or Visual-Proactive assistance. Analysis of 2,140 tutor messages showed that visual access shifted assistance toward checking ongoing work, while proactivity enhanced error identification and directive hints. Learners valued feedback grounded in their writing; those who received proactive help rated it as supportive, and about a third wanted it more often. These findings inform when tutors should intervene and what they should address. We release the platform, prompts, and instruments, together with 255,984 timestamped images of handwritten work linked to tutoring conversations, intervention decisions, and learning outcomes, to support multimodal tutoring systems that preserve the affordances of handwritten work while providing adaptive feedback.

infographic.key_insight: Live visual access to handwritten mathematics shifted AI tutoring toward checking ongoing work, while proactive assistance increased error identification and directive hints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Camera-enabled tutoring systems can ground feedback in handwritten reasoning, making intervention timing and feedback targeting important design choices.
method: Built a multimodal tutoring platform with a live phone-camera view of paper-based work.
Randomized 117 adults solving calculus problems to Text-Reactive, Visual-Reactive, or Visual-Proactive assistance.
Analyzed tutor messages and learner feedback across conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study analyzed 2,140 tutor messages; released resources include 255,984 timestamped handwriting images linked to conversations, intervention decisions, and learning outcomes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports feedback patterns and learner perceptions, but does not establish improved learning outcomes or generalization beyond adults solving calculus problems.
infographic.paper_title: Exploring Visual Access and Proactive AI Tutoring for Handwritten Mathematics

title: LowNet: Looped Wavelet Neural Networks with 24 Learnable Parameters for Solving Poisson Equations
authors: Yuanhao Gong
abstract: Poisson equations frequently appear in various fields, such as mathematics, physics and informatics. Solving Poisson equation, however, is challenging. Traditional methods are not data-specific, although have high certainty. They require a large number of iterations due to the CFL numerical stability. In contrast, deep learning methods are data-driven and more efficient, but require accurate training data and suffer from heavy computation. To tackle these issues, we propose a wavelet-inspired Poisson solver with 24 trainable scalars. The proposed network has several advantages. First, it is compact. It has four independent $5\times5$ kernels, each represented by six parameters, leading to 24 scalars in total. Such compact format can be deployed on most devices. Second, thanks to the loop design, it achieves higher accuracy than previous methods. A residual loop reuses the wavelet block without increasing its parameters. Numerical experiments confirm that such loop indeed improves the solving accuracy. On 10000 images, one, two, and three loops of the wavelet block lead to PSNRs of $47.27$, $74.14$, and $100.74$ dB, respectively. Third, the proposed method is computationally fast. Thanks to the wavelet transform, the proposed method has linear computation complexity, leading to high computation performance. In short, we propose a novel looped wavelet neural network with compactness, accuracy and efficiency for solving Poisson equations. Our method can be applied in various fields, such as computational fluid dynamics, image reconstruction, biomedical engineering, electromagnetic field simulation.

infographic.key_insight: LowNet uses a looped, wavelet-inspired neural network with just 24 trainable scalars to solve Poisson equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its compact parameterization and claimed linear computational complexity could support efficient Poisson solvers for simulation and image reconstruction.
method: Represent four independent 5×5 kernels with six parameters each.
Reuse the wavelet block through residual loops without adding trainable parameters.
Use wavelet transforms for linear computational complexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 10,000 images, the abstract reports PSNRs of 47.27, 74.14, and 100.74 dB for one, two, and three loops, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalization across boundary conditions, geometries, or engineering-scale problems; additional loops also require extra computation.
infographic.paper_title: LowNet: Looped Wavelet Neural Networks with 24 Learnable Parameters for Solving Poisson Equations

title: Hybrid metaheuristics for architectural design optimization under small evaluation and wall-clock budgets
authors: Luciano Ambrosini
abstract: Architectural and structural design optimization in parametric software affords about a thousand evaluations of an expensive model for problems with tens of variables, a regime for which most metaheuristics were not designed. On the side of artificial intelligence, two hybrid metaheuristics are proposed: a covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) whose sampling is enriched with differential-evolution trial vectors, and a particle swarm with success-history parameter adaptation, differential-evolution injection and local refinement. A budget-aware delay of population-size reduction in adaptive differential evolution is also proposed. Under a hard cap of 1,200 evaluations, all counted, the CMA-ES hybrid ranks first on seven shifted and rotated functions at 10 and 30 variables and beats CMA-ES on six of seven functions at 30 variables. Ablations attribute this gain to the injection and show that a local search pays off only when its result re-enters the population. The delayed schedule improves three adaptive differential-evolution variants in 40 of 51 comparisons, with no loss. On the side of engineering application, in Grasshopper the CMA-ES hybrid and plain CMA-ES are never significantly worse than the optimizers of Galapagos, SilverEye, Opossum and Tunny on travelling-salesman instances and on a built 85-variable free-form shell, where they end 48 % below the best external tool in 15 minutes. On a 22-variable building-performance problem with binary choices, differential evolution leads instead. Shifting and rotating the functions reverses the rank of Harris hawks optimization. Solvers should therefore be selected by problem structure and stopping time, not by a single ranking.

infographic.key_insight: Under tight evaluation budgets, enriching CMA-ES with differential-evolution trial vectors improves optimization, but solver choice still depends on problem structure and stopping time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Budget-aware hybrid optimizers can improve expensive parametric architectural and structural design searches within practical wall-clock limits.
method: Inject differential-evolution trial vectors into CMA-ES sampling.
Combine particle swarm optimization with success-history adaptation, differential-evolution injection and local refinement.
Delay population-size reduction in adaptive differential evolution to suit small evaluation budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: With all evaluations counted under a 1,200-evaluation cap, the CMA-ES hybrid ranked first across seven shifted and rotated benchmarks at 10 and 30 variables; in a 15-minute, 85-variable shell-design test, it and plain CMA-ES achieved final objective values 48% below the best external tool.
infographic.watch_item: Do not assume a universal winner: differential evolution led on the mixed-binary building problem, and local refinement helped only when its result re-entered the population.
infographic.paper_title: Hybrid metaheuristics for architectural design optimization under small evaluation and wall-clock budgets

title: Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint Denoising for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Zilei Shao, Ian Li, Heng Zhao, Kewei Lian, Guy Van den Broeck, Zhe Zeng
abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. Decoding heuristics reduce the resulting errors by controlling which tokens are committed, but leave the underlying distribution factorized. Joint modeling addresses the source of the problem, yet existing methods attach separately learned layers to frozen denoisers, leaving the backbone unadapted to the joint objective and the coupling parameters fixed across contexts. We propose Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser combining a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer. Given a partially masked input, the Transformer produces token potentials that shape per-position predictions and compact gates that modulate the layer's coupling parameters, yielding a context-dependent joint distribution while retaining exact conditional inference. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. At inference, Codpula supports standard heuristics and uses conditional queries to adapt commitments to dependencies among proposed tokens without extra Transformer evaluations within a step. Codpula sets new state-of-the-art results across a broad suite of reasoning benchmarks while advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

infographic.key_insight: Codpula replaces independent parallel token predictions with a context-dependent joint distribution that captures dependencies between tokens.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Dependency-aware parallel decoding could improve accuracy–latency trade-offs for mathematical reasoning and code generation.
method: A Transformer produces per-token potentials and context-dependent gates that modulate a tractable probabilistic layer.
Both components are trained jointly with a conditional denoising objective and a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters.
Exact conditional queries guide token commitments without extra Transformer evaluations within a decoding step.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art results across reasoning benchmarks and an improved accuracy–latency Pareto frontier for math and code, but provides no benchmark names or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The probabilistic layer adds inference and training complexity; its overhead and scalability require validation beyond the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint Denoising for Diffusion Language Models

title: Computing Fréchet Means on Unknown Submanifolds of Riemannian Manifolds
authors: Ian McPherson, Mauro Maggioni
abstract: Empirical averages are fundamental statistical primitives. On nonlinear spaces, their generalization, the Fréchet mean, generally lacks a closed-form solution, and its computation requires solving an optimization problem. We study the computation of intrinsic Fréchet means for data supported on an unknown compact $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $M_{1}$ embedded in an ambient metric space $(X,d_{\operatorname{obs}})$. Such settings arise when observations are better represented in non-Euclidean spaces, like probability distributions in Wasserstein space. We assume access only to a local sampler on $M_{1}$ and the observation metric $d_{\operatorname{obs}}$, without knowledge of its intrinsic geometry. We propose a graph-based iterative algorithm that adaptively samples the manifold and approximates geodesic interpolation. Under mild assumptions, we establish an $O(1/T)$ expected objective gap guarantee using at most $\widetilde{O}(T^{4d+3})$ sampled points. As a byproduct of our analysis we extend the metric equivalence guarantees of ISOMAP from Euclidean to Riemannian ambient spaces, which may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for computing intrinsic averages on unknown data manifolds.

infographic.key_insight: Intrinsic Fréchet means on unknown manifolds can be approximated using only local sampling and observed distances, without knowing the intrinsic geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method enables geometry-aware averaging of nonlinear data, including probability distributions represented in Wasserstein space.
method: Adaptively sample the unknown manifold and build a distance-based graph.
Approximate geodesic interpolation for iterative Fréchet mean optimization.
Extend ISOMAP metric-equivalence guarantees to Riemannian ambient spaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under stated assumptions, the analysis guarantees an O(1/T) expected objective gap using at most Õ(T^(4d+3)) sampled points; numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness.
infographic.watch_item: The sample bound grows steeply with intrinsic dimension d, raising scalability concerns despite the convergence guarantee.
infographic.paper_title: Computing Fréchet Means on Unknown Submanifolds of Riemannian Manifolds
